headline: High risk of prompt injection, data leakage, and cascading errors from filesystem-bridged desktop automation into a plugin-driven orchestration kernel.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Agent A reads/writes the whole local filesystem and clipboard, while Agent B can ingest files and use MCP/OpenAPI plugins. A can therefore place attacker-controlled content where B may treat it as instructions. The shared filesystem bridge makes this more than manual copy-paste, and B’s plugin-driven tool use increases hijack risk.
conditions: IF Agent B reads content produced by Agent A from the shared filesystem or memory store without provenance checks, injection is plausible.
IF Agent A is run with --auto_run or equivalent unattended execution, malicious content can be propagated faster.
mitigations: Disable unattended execution on Agent A; require confirmation for every code block.
Isolate the shared workspace into per-agent directories.
Add provenance tags and reject untrusted instructions in Agent B.
Restrict Agent B plugins to allowlisted, read-only operations for the first run.
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and instruction/data separation before B consumes A outputs.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent A can access anything reachable on the local machine, including files and clipboard, and Agent B can send context to Azure OpenAI/OpenAI/Hugging Face or MCP/OpenAPI tools. If sensitive local data reaches B, its default API-backed processing can exfiltrate it outside the machine. The pair therefore creates a strong leakage path in default use.
conditions: IF Agent A is pointed at a directory containing secrets or regulated data, that data can enter the pair.
IF Agent B is configured with third-party model providers or external MCP/OpenAPI tools, the data can leave the local environment.
mitigations: Run both agents only on a scrubbed test workspace.
Remove or disable external model providers for the first session.
Block network egress for Agent B except to approved endpoints.
Separate secrets into a directory Agent A cannot read.
requires-engineering: enforce data-loss-prevention filters before any B API call.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Agent A has unrestricted filesystem write and git-state modification, while Agent B also has filesystem write and shared state via memory store. Both can mutate overlapping resources without a documented locking mechanism, so concurrent writes can corrupt files, git history, or shared state. The conflict is direct and default-enabled.
conditions: IF both agents target the same working tree or shared directory, write conflicts are possible.
IF Agent A modifies git state while Agent B writes related files, repository corruption or inconsistent commits can occur.
mitigations: Assign separate working directories to each agent.
Serialize all writes through a single operator-controlled queue.
Disable git writes for one agent during collaborative runs.
Take a snapshot before either agent starts mutating files.
requires-engineering: add distributed locking around shared filesystem and memory-store writes.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Agent B is an orchestration layer that can treat Agent A’s outputs as inputs to plugins or actions, while Agent A can generate arbitrary shell output and filesystem artifacts. Without a verification step, A’s mistakes can be amplified by B into downstream tool calls or persisted artifacts. This is a default interaction risk, not a niche configuration issue.
conditions: IF Agent B forwards Agent A output into a plugin or API call without validation, errors can cascade.
IF Agent A produces malformed commands, paths, or facts that B trusts, downstream actions may be wrong or harmful.
mitigations: Insert a human review step before B acts on A output.
Require schema validation on all A-to-B messages.
Limit B to read-only summarization until outputs are verified.
Log and diff A outputs before any downstream action.
requires-engineering: implement typed contracts between A and B.

E_compliance.rationale: Agent A touches anything reachable on the local machine, while Agent B can send context to third-party model providers and plugin credentials. The profiles do not specify residency, HIPAA, or DPA guarantees, so compliance mismatch is plausible but not proven. Uncertainty here should not be treated as benign because the data classes are broad and the egress paths are explicit.
conditions: IF regulated data is present on the local machine, Agent A can access it.
IF Agent B is configured with non-approved external providers, residency or retention obligations may be violated.
mitigations: Restrict both agents to non-regulated sample data.
Use only approved regional model endpoints.
Review provider retention settings before first run.
Disable plugin credentials until compliance review is complete.
requires-engineering: document and enforce residency/retention controls per data class.
